Departures & Arrivals
When a population point moves, the settlement it leaves loses a worked tile, the migrants travel for one or more turns, and the settlement they join places the point when they arrive.
Leaving

Each departing point removes one of the settlement's outlying rural improvements and that tile's yields. Pillaged tiles go first. A starving city keeps its food tiles longest. Otherwise plain tiles go before resource tiles, and distant plots before near ones. Cultural Enclave tiles are exempt. The emptied rural district is then cleared so the city can grow onto the tile again.

A settlement loses at most two points per turn on the default Medium preset. A single siege displaces at most 60% of the population the city had when it began, and a single disaster at most 50%. Deaths from a long crisis (see When There Is No Refuge) fall outside these caps.
On the Road

Travel time grows with distance, up to four turns by default, and slower game speeds stretch it. War refugees always spend at least one turn on the road. If their destination is captured or razed while they travel, or stays too full to receive them, they die in transit and count as losses.
A settlement takes in at most four newcomers per turn by default. The rest wait and try again next turn, longest-waiting first.
Arriving

Other civilizations place their own arrivals. For your cities, the How newcomers settle setting (Options, Add-ons, Emigration, Advanced settings, Arrivals & departures) decides what happens:[BLIST][LI][B]Ask me[/B] (default): a Newcomers or Refugees pop-up in the receiving city lets you pick the tile, let the city decide, or wait. Three switches choose which kinds of arrival ask; by default only refugees ask, and migrants and returning people are placed at once.[LI][B]Automatic[/B]: the city places the point immediately, as it does when it grows.[LI][B]Migrant unit[/B]: the newcomers arrive as a Migrant unit beside the city for you to resettle. An unsettled Migrant costs upkeep every turn.[LI][B]Off[/B]: the game's own Grow City prompt asks you to place the point.[/LIST]

The Refugees pop-up names where the arrivals fled from and what they fled, with a quotation in their people's voice (see Voices of the Displaced). Refugees from a civilization you have not met are described only as displaced.

Each of your settlements has a "Dissuade newcomers" button on its Settlements card, with its price in the button. While it's on, people who would have moved there choose again by the same pull as everyone else: another of your settlements, another civilization's, or staying where they are when nowhere else is better. You lose the ones who go abroad or stay home. People already on the road still arrive. It costs 1 Influence a turn, and when you can't pay, newcomers are welcome there again. "Welcome newcomers" undoes it. AI civilizations do the same: one past its congestion bar dissuades newcomers in an unhappy settlement that has been taking people in, pays the same upkeep, and welcomes them again once the pressure eases.
Refugees Waiting to Settle

One in five war and disaster refugees (by default) settles on arrival. The rest enter a waiting pool at their destination and settle over the following turns. A happy, open, uncrowded host settles them faster; an Anti-Immigration Stance slows them. The host pays upkeep for those still waiting. If the crisis they fled reaches the new city, the waiting refugees move on first. The city readout and the City Details panel show how many are waiting.
The Cost of Taking People In

Each newcomer adds an integration load to the receiving civilization, which fades over about six to eight turns. While it lasts, the civilization pays [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold each turn and its accumulated [icon:YIELD_HAPPINESS] Happiness is drawn down, delaying its next Celebration. A civilization settling many arrivals also attracts fewer new ones. Each of these costs can be set to 0 in Advanced settings; see Integration & the Cost of Growth.
How an Enclave Grows

A foreign community grows into an enclave in three stages: Foothold, Established and Recognized. Each settlement is measured by its largest community from another civilization. The city readout shows the stage, what the next one takes and anything holding it back, and the enclave's tile tooltip and the Settlements tab use the same names.
Foothold
A community has a foothold once it makes up 25% of a settlement and has at least 3 population of its own. The Chronicle notes it. Nothing appears on the map yet.
Established

At 30% of the settlement, or at 6 population whatever its share (scaled to how large settlements are in your game), the community is established and its enclave forms: a tile at the city's edge, named for its people, giving its own yield from the first turn.
Recognized

Once the community has stayed established for 8 turns, with dips of up to 3 turns forgiven, the enclave is recognized. Its stance is chosen, by the city or by you through a pop-up when enclave recognition is set to Ask me, and pays once.
How an Enclave Ends

An enclave fades when its people stay below 12.5% of the settlement, and below the size bar, for 12 turns; the city readout counts the turns down. It also ends when its tile is built over or the city is razed; a community whose enclave was built over stays, and forms a new one once it has held together for the dwell period again. If a city-state or independent takes the settlement, the enclave is set aside until a civilization holds the city again. War with its homeland makes an enclave contested, which changes what it gives but not its stage.
Limits

Each civilization forms at most 3 enclaves an age and holds at most two from any one people across its cities. When you're asked to recognize enclaves, decisions are at least 12 turns apart and at most 3 an age. A civilization that hasn't formed an enclave as an age goes on sees its bars come down, up to 40%, until one forms. All of these are set under Cultural enclaves in Advanced settings.
Coming Home

People driven out of one of your settlements keep their tie to it. The Left pane of that settlement's card on the Settlements tab lists everyone away: how many, where they live now and since when, the tiles their departure tore down, what a returnee is worth at home (the yields of a rural tile there), when they come home on their own, and two buttons that bring them back sooner for a price. A settlement you no longer hold is listed with its people staying where they are.

Once a settlement your people fled is calm enough for them to return and at least five of your people are displaced from settlements you still hold, a small pop-up offers to open the Settlements tab, wait, or stop reminding you. It comes back only once half again as many are displaced and ten turns have passed. "Displaced-people reminders" under Options, Add-ons, Emigration is the same switch, and the threshold is an Advanced setting.
On Their Own

People who fled war, conquest or a disaster into another of your settlements can go home by themselves once it's safe. People who left over unhappiness, or because another settlement drew them away, stay where they settled, and so do people who went to another civilization unless you call them from abroad. Home has to be calm for 3 turns in a row, without war, siege, disaster, famine, unrest or war weariness, or for 10 turns after fighting inside its borders or a siege, because a frontier settlement hit once is likely to be hit again.

Not everyone goes back. When home is calm, each group decides once how many of them return. After an absence of up to 5 turns, 80% go back. For each turn after that, 2% fewer go back, down to 30%, and a quarter fewer when the settlement they live in now is clearly better off than home. The rest settle where they are, and the Left pane shows them as staying. Hasten can still bring them back for a price. People driven out again later decide the next time home is calm.

Every 4 turns, one of those going back comes home, plus one more for every 8 still coming, and settles the plot their people left when it's still open, otherwise another free plot of the settlement. The Chronicle and a notice beside End Turn say how many are coming and how many stayed, and again when the last of them is back. AI civilizations follow the same rule. "People find their own way home" in Advanced settings holds the numbers and an off switch.
Hasten

Hasten pays [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold or [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence to bring people living elsewhere in your civilization back now instead of over the next turns. Exactly the number paid for come, largest group first. The card names the tile a returnee works at home and the tiles they leave where they live now, the net per person, and how many turns sooner the fee brings them; the price buttons' hover carries the full ledger. Inside your borders a return swaps one tile for another, so the fee buys time. Each settlement runs its own cooldown, so hastening one does not lock the others.
Call from Abroad

Call from abroad pays for a call to your people living in another civilization's cities. It is a gamble: each person asked answers with the odds shown (about 18% by default), rolled one by one, and you pay for the size you chose whatever comes of it. Every person who answers is a tile gained for good. The hover gives the odds and the cost per person who comes. An unanswered call is written into the Chronicle and still starts the cooldown. People with an enclave of their own rarely return by themselves, so a call is the reliable way to bring them back.
Prices and Cooldowns

A call is one person, about half of those callable, or everyone, in [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold or [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence; a price the treasury cannot cover is greyed. Price rises faster than head count: two people cost nearly three times one, three about five times. Calls abroad cost more, and each age past Antiquity multiplies the price (x3 in the Exploration Age, x9 in the Modern Age). After a call, the same settlement waits eight turns before calling again. Only people whose home and host settlements both still stand under the owners they had when they left can be called.

AI civilizations pay the same prices, less a discount for the game's difficulty (4% a level of the Gold handicap, so 20% off at Deity), and while homecoming is on they only pay to call people abroad. When a call takes people out of one of your cities, you get a notice and a Chronicle line naming who called. Prices, odds and the AI's part are set under Calling people home in Advanced settings.
Treatment of Communities

How a host treats the foreign communities in its cities follows its immigration stance. The two stance cards are policy cards like any other, open to every civilization. Each one takes a policy slot of your own.
[B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B]: an enclave recognized while you're at war with its homeland keeps 100% of its yields instead of 50%, and war and disaster refugees choose your cities first.

[B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B]: every enclave you recognize keeps 50% of its yields, 25% at war with its homeland. Slot both stances and their effects on migration and enclaves cancel out, and neither brings a slot.

[B]Consular Protection[/B] (Exploration and Modern Ages) gives +3 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence each turn (+5 in the Modern Age), and +1 more for every recognized enclave of your people in another civilization's cities, up to +4. When a civilization hosting one of those enclaves slots an Anti-Immigration Stance, you hold grievances against it, once per host per age.

When war first reaches an enclave, the Chronicle names the host's stance: an Anti-Immigration Stance falls hardest on the families, a Pro-Immigration Stance holds. With the Partisans mod running, the stance also sets how fast an enclave's unrest builds in wartime.
Immigration Policies

Emigration adds ten policy cards: the two stances in every age, and Talent Attraction and Consular Protection from the Exploration Age on. They slot and swap like any other card and stack with an Open Borders agreement, which raises migration both ways between the two signatories. Each card's yields are native game effects, which is also what the AI's planner values a card by; its migration effect comes from the mod. The two stances name their downsides on the card: the Pro-Immigration Stance's integration cost per newcomer and the enclaves that come with arrivals, the Anti-Immigration Stance's lost growth and tiles and the half of enclave yields given up.
Antiquity Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Citizenship): +1 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per turn; +50% immigration; refugees come to you first; enclaves keep 100% of their yields at war.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Citizenship): +2 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -2 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per turn; -60% immigration, -40% emigration; refugees settle 60% slower; enclaves keep 50% of their yields.[/LIST]
Exploration Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Economics): +2 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per turn; +50% immigration; refugees come to you first; enclaves keep 100% of their yields at war.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Economics): +3 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -3 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per turn; -60% immigration, -40% emigration; refugees settle 60% slower; enclaves keep 50% of their yields.[LI][B]Talent Attraction[/B] (Inspiration): +1 [icon:YIELD_SCIENCE] Science per 5 [icon:YIELD_POPULATION] Population and -2 [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold in every settlement.[LI][B]Consular Protection[/B] (Diplomatic Service): +3 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per turn, and +1 more for each recognized enclave of your people abroad, up to +4; grievances against a host that slots an Anti-Immigration Stance.[/LIST]
Modern Age

[BLIST][LI][B]Pro-Immigration Stance[/B] (Social Question): +3 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per turn; +50% immigration; refugees come to you first; enclaves keep 100% of their yields at war.[LI][B]Anti-Immigration Stance[/B] (Social Question): +4 [icon:YIELD_PRODUCTION] Production in every city, -4 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per turn; -60% immigration, -40% emigration; refugees settle 60% slower; enclaves keep 50% of their yields.[LI][B]Talent Attraction[/B] (Modernization): +1 [icon:YIELD_SCIENCE] Science per 4 [icon:YIELD_POPULATION] Population and -3 [icon:YIELD_GOLD] Gold in every settlement.[LI][B]Consular Protection[/B] (Political Theory): +5 [icon:YIELD_DIPLOMACY] Influence per turn, and +1 more for each recognized enclave of your people abroad, up to +4; grievances against a host that slots an Anti-Immigration Stance.[/LIST]

Talent Attraction pays by population through the game's own yield system, so it shows in each settlement's yield breakdown, grows with every immigrant who settles and keeps paying after the inflow stops; its Gold upkeep per settlement shows there too, so a wide civilization pays more for it. Pair it with a Pro-Immigration Stance or an Open Borders agreement to fill your settlements faster.
Map Lenses

Emigration adds two lenses to the game's lens panel, each with a hotkey. Both follow the Spoil Guard (see Scope & Visibility). While a lens is up, the game's tile tooltip is hidden and the lens shows its own readout under the cursor.
Prosperity Lens (Shift+P)

The Prosperity lens paints each settled tile by what stands on it. A tile's score is the sum of:[BLIST][LI]a wonder on the hex: +6[LI]the city center: +3[LI]each building: +2, and +1 for a completed quarter[LI]a worked improvement: +1[LI]the hex's own yield: +1 per 3[LI]a river: +1[LI]a natural wonder: +3 on the hex, +2 for each next door[LI]a wonder next door: +1 each[LI]anything pillaged: -3 each on the hex, -1 each next door[/LIST]The scale is the same in every settlement and is banded: Flourishing (8 or more), Thriving (5 to 7), Ordinary (2 to 4), Meager (0 to 1) and Blighted (below 0), on gray-to-green and gray-to-red gradients. Water with nothing built on it is left unpainted.

Hovering a tile shows its band, score and every term behind it, then the settlement's Prosperity score, whether it is gaining or losing people, and why. Wonders and natural wonders are read from the game's database, so ones added by an age or another mod count too.
Ethnic Composition Lens (Shift+E)

Each settlement records the civilization each of its people descends from. The Ethnic Composition lens draws that record as a per-tile mosaic. The urban core takes the dominant origin's color. Each smaller community gets a number of tiles in proportion to its share, densest tiles first, in a paler color the smaller it is. A community with a Cultural Enclave is placed on the enclave's tile first. Without an enclave, a tile's color is capped at the share an enclave requires, so a community below that share shows as a lighter tint. Hover a settled tile for its exact mix.
Enclave Markers

An enclave tile uses the model of the improvement it stands in for, so it carries a marker with the origin civilization's symbol. Hovering the tile shows the enclave's tooltip in place of the improvement's: the enclave's name and stage (established, recognized, contested or fading), the tile's yields and their sources, what the enclave's people built there, what the replaced improvement still pays the city, and the stance the city took when it recognized the enclave.
Notifications & the City Readout
Notices Beside End Turn

Migration news arrives in the game's own notification train beside End Turn, each kind with its own icon: people leaving your settlements, newcomers settling in them, your people coming home, a refugee crisis abroad, a disaster displacing people, and a civilization you have met opening or closing its borders. The text sits in the icon's hover, a click opens the Emigration screen on the tab that matters, and a right-click dismisses it. Counts are shown in population points, in people, or both, for example 3 population points (36,000 people), set by the Population unit of measurement option. Disasters carry the game's event names, wars their names, and conquests the name of the city taken. An arrival notice ends with what the newcomers cost you each turn.

By default only the largest event of each migration pass is announced, with cooldowns and thresholds on top. The Notifications section of Advanced settings switches to one notice per cause, or to none, and can bring back the mod's own stacked on-screen toasts. Every notification goes to the log either way.
The Notifications Log

The Notifications tab of the Migration dashboard keeps the last 120 notifications, newest first: the turn, the cause and named event, the settlement people left, where they went, and how many. Each entry expands to its detail. Migration Chronicle entries (an exodus, a diaspora taking root, a homecoming, an enclave recognized or faded, a stance taken by another civilization, each refugee decision and each call home) appear in the same list.
The City Readout

Selecting one of your cities shows a small migration panel: the pressures on it (unhappiness, war, disaster, famine, overcrowding), whether it is gaining or losing people and how fast, where leavers are likely to go, what would stop them ("What would stop it: +3 Food or +2 Happiness here (Granary gives +1 Food)", from the same model that scores the settlement, with the building of the age that gives most of that yield), what its newcomers cost your civilization each turn, refugees waiting to settle, and progress toward a Cultural Enclave. A warning marks a city whose people have nowhere to flee. The Settlements tab of the dashboard shows the same for every settlement at once.
City Details

The game's City Details panel gains two Emigration sections. Under Citizen Growth: the city's people by origin, emigration by destination, immigration by origin, and refugees awaiting settlement. Under Building Breakdown: the city's Cultural Enclave, if it has one. Both update as you switch cities.
Options & Intensity

Emigration's settings are under Options, Add-ons, in the main menu and in game. The Add-ons tab holds the everyday settings, and the Advanced settings button opens the rest. Changes apply immediately or at the next migration pass.
Intensity Presets

The Intensity preset sets the per-turn limits, how far people travel, and how strongly violence pushes them out.[BLIST][LI][B]Low[/B]: rare, small movements; at most one point out and two in per city per turn; slow siege displacement.[LI][B]Medium[/B] (default): at most two out and four in per city per turn.[LI][B]High[/B]: frequent, large movements; up to four out and eight in per city per turn, faster flight and heavier war surges.[/LIST]Changing a preset-controlled setting in Advanced settings shows the preset as Custom.
Everyday Settings

[BLIST][LI][B]Population unit of measurement[/B]: population points, historically scaled people (matching the Demographics mod), or both.[LI][B]Movement between civilizations[/B] and three [B]Refugees from conflict[/B] sliders (overall, wars between major powers, raids by minor powers) scale those flows alone.[LI][B]Dashboard data[/B]: live migration, or sample data to preview the network. [B]Migration timeline detail[/B]: how often the network records a timeline snapshot. [B]Simplify dashboard[/B]: hides the Network diagram. [B]Dashboard dock button[/B].[LI]On/off switches for [B]notifications[/B], [B]ethnic integration[/B] and [B]return migration[/B], and one for each decision pop-up: [B]Refugee decisions[/B], [B]Newcomer placement decisions[/B], [B]Displaced-people reminders[/B] and [B]Enclave stance decisions[/B]. With a switch off the mod decides for you, and the Settlements tab still works.[LI][B]First-loss explainer[/B]: off by default. On, the first time one of your settlements loses a tile to emigration, one page says what happened, where they went and why, what happens next and where to look. Once per game. [LI][B]Spoil Guard[/B]: on by default, hides civilizations you have not met across the Emigration screens (see Scope & Visibility).[/LIST]
Advanced Settings

The Advanced settings window holds every individual setting, more than a hundred, in collapsible sections: Pacing, Scope, Border policies, Prosperity model, War & violence, Disasters, Geography & movement, Integration costs, Balance brakes, Arrivals & departures, Cultural enclaves, Calling people home, Attrition, Notifications, Readouts & rankings and Visuals. Sections you open stay open. Values show their units (55%, x1.5, 3 turns) or a word (Off, Instant). The window has a search box, a marker on each changed setting, a reset for each, and Reset all. Per-leader and per-civilization tuning (see Leaders & Civilizations) has its own switch here.
Game Speed

Every turn count in the mod scales with game speed, from Online to Marathon: cooldowns, transit time, integration periods, enclave dwell and fade clocks, and decision cooldowns. A Marathon game sees the same migrations spread over proportionally more turns. Population counts stay the same at every speed.
The Demographics Mod

Emigration runs on its own. With the Demographics mod installed, it also adds an Emigration tab to the Demographics screen and shares its population scaling, so a population point means the same number of people in both. The Migration dashboard's tabs appear there as sub-tabs, and the Migration page in Demographics opens the dashboard.
Graphs and Tables

[BLIST][LI][B]Net Migration (Graph)[/B]: cumulative arrivals minus departures, by civilization.[LI][B]Net Migration (Table)[/B]: the same value as a diverging bar, beside departures and arrivals split into Internal (between a civilization's own settlements), External (across a border, which is what Net measures) and Total.[LI][B]Emigration[/B] and [B]Immigration[/B]: gross outflow and inflow, broken down by cause.[LI][B]Refugees (Left / Arrived)[/B]: displaced people sent and received, with optional war and disaster markers on the timeline.[/LIST]A Data section toggles the metrics and the unit (scaled people or population points). Demographics' war-effects tooltip can show a Refugees row from Emigration's numbers.
Voices of the Displaced

Each pop-up about refugees, migrants, a returning diaspora or a settled foreign community carries a short quotation in the voice of that people: a refugee, exile or migrant of theirs where such words survive, otherwise a witness who wrote of them with dignity. Each civilization's page lists its quotations, where each appears, and who the speaker was.
Where the Voices Appear

[BLIST][LI][B]The refugee decision[/B] (Refugees at the Border, The Sick at the Gates) and [B]the Refugees pop-up[/B]: a refugee's words from the people fleeing.[LI][B]The Newcomers pop-up[/B]: a migrant's words from their people.[LI][B]The reminder that your people can come home[/B]: someone of your own civilization who longed for home or came back to it.[LI][B]The Cultural Enclave decision[/B]: a line from the enclave people's own writers, inscriptions or proverbs; a people's first and second enclaves in your empire each have their own line.[/LIST]The event fixes the line, so reloading a save shows the same words. When a people has no line for a situation, or comes from a civilization you have not met, the pop-up uses the general pools on the Voices of Many Lands page, which name no people.
How the Quotations Were Chosen

Every line was checked against a readable copy of its source. Cuts are marked with an ellipsis. A published translation names its translator; (trans.) alone marks the mod's own rendering of the verified original. Enclave lines come from a people's own writers, inscriptions and proverbs. Refugee and migrant lines come from a refugee, exile or migrant of that people, or else a witness who wrote of them with dignity.

Lines that stereotype a people, cast the displaced as invaders, a burden or a threat, quote a perpetrator of atrocities or a hate figure, trivialize sacred text, or dwell on graphic trauma were excluded. The full source record, including rejected lines, is published with the mod's documentation.
Original Languages

A quotation from a non-English source shows the original beside an English rendering. Latin-script originals appear in full, from Old English and Old Norse to Vietnamese, Turkish and the transliterated Akkadian of the Assyrian inscriptions. Originals in Arabic, Hebrew, Greek, Cyrillic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Georgian, Mongolian, the Indic and Southeast Asian scripts, and Chinese, Japanese and Korean are shown in English only, because the game's fonts lack those scripts.
About Emigration

Emigration is a user-interface mod. Each turn it reads the state of the world and writes population, tiles, yields and Influence back through the game's own commands. Its own database rows add the policy cards, the notification types, this Civilopedia section and two city strategies the game's AI can switch on; base-game rules and files are left as they are. It simulates every living major civilization from the first turn, met or unmet. The Common Questions page is the short version of what drives migration.

Version 4.0.0, for Civilization VII 1.5.0. The interface is available in twelve languages. The source, the full documentation with every formula, and the record of every quotation's source are on GitHub at github.com/tmtmiller1/civilizationvii-emigration.
The People Behind the Numbers

This mod turns migration and displacement into game systems. In reality people most often leave home because of war, persecution, disaster or hardship. The mod presents refugees as people, lets the displaced speak in their own words wherever those words survive, and counts a stricken city's losses as deaths. The author has marked the mod's milestones with donations to refugee relief. If you are able, consider supporting UNHCR, the International Rescue Committee, Médecins Sans Frontières, the International Refugee Assistance Project, or local refugee and mutual-aid groups.
Credits

Emigration is by Tower. Its Prosperity model adapts the Emigration mod for Civilization V by killmeplease, Tomahawk, Mk Z and Tim_The_Texan. Population scaling matches the Demographics mod, and the Talent Raid diplomacy actions come from the Diplomacy Extended mod. Quotations are drawn from the published sources listed in the mod's documentation; translations marked (trans.) without a translator's name are the mod's own.
